activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Muslims perform the ritual prayer, salah, five times a day, facing the Kaaba in Mecca.
story:
The cultural festival smelled like fried plantains, incense, and somebody's burnt popcorn, and Marcus had already eaten two samosas when his stomach growled anyway. His friend Mariam was standing near the folding tables with her phone out, spinning slowly in a circle like a human compass.

"What are you doing, a dance?" Marcus asked.

"Finding east-northeast," Mariam said. "It's time for salah, the ritual prayer, and Muslims pray facing the Kaaba in Mecca, five times a day. Problem is, this hall has no windows and my phone compass is being weird near the stage speakers."

Marcus peered at her screen, which showed a wobbling arrow. He tested an idea. "The speakers are magnets, right? Maybe the compass works better over here, away from the sound system." He walked twenty steps toward the food tables, held out the phone, and watched the arrow steady itself and settle. "Ha! It was the speakers. Come look."

Mariam followed him, checked the direction against a backup compass on her keychain, and smiled. "Close enough. Good detective work." She laid her jacket on the carpet near the folding chairs, and while she prayed, Marcus stood quietly beside the samosa table, feeling awkward and impressed at the same time. A little kid nearby wailed because his balloon had escaped toward the luminous paper lanterns strung across the ceiling, and Marcus caught the string just before it hit a hot lamp. "There," he said, handing it back. The kid sniffled and hugged the balloon like a rescued organism that needed care.

When Mariam stood up, she laughed at the balloon drama. "You consoled him faster than my mom consoles me when I lose at checkers."

"That's my talent," Marcus said. "Balloon rescue and compass science." He checked his watch, then his stomach, which growled again, loud enough that Lucille, arranging pup petri dishes at the science booth, snorted with laughter across the hall.

"Third samosa?" Mariam offered him one from her pocket. "You've earned it, detective."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A guinea pig's front teeth never stop growing, so it needs things to chew on to wear them down.
story:
Luca knelt by the cage in the shelter's small animal room, watching a brown guinea pig named Biscuit chew on the bars of her enclosure. The sound was loud for such a small animal, a steady clang, clang, clang. "Why does she do that?" Luca asked Aydin, who was crouched beside him.

"She hates the cage," Aydin said. "She's trying to rebel and break out." That sounded possible, but Luca wasn't sure. He'd read the little card taped to the front of the cage, and one line of it stuck in his head: a guinea pig's front teeth never stop growing. That meant something, though he couldn't yet say what. When Ms. Bear, the shelter's small animal keeper, walked past with a stack of clean towels, Luca asked her if Biscuit was trying to escape.

"Sometimes teeth, sometimes boredom," Ms. Bear said, and kept walking. That wasn't much of an answer. Luca thought about the fact on the card. If her front teeth never stopped growing, she would need to wear them down somehow, and chewing on metal bars would do it. He remembered being biased toward Aydin's escape theory just because it was more dramatic, and now he felt a little foolish about it. "Let's test it," he said. He found a cardboard tube in the supply bin and pushed it through the bars of the cage.

Biscuit stopped clanging almost at once. She gripped the tube in her paws and gnawed it in long, rasping strips, working her front teeth the whole time. Aydin laughed. "Okay, so she's not staging a prison break."

Luca carried the guinea pig, now his, out to the front desk in a cardboard carrier. He'd asked for a pet for two years, and his parents had finally said yes this morning. He had imagined this moment as the climax of the whole day, and it was, but not in the way he'd pictured. It was quieter. He added a bag of wooden chew sticks and three more cardboard tubes to the pile on the counter, paying for them with the birthday money in his pocket. The cashier raised her eyebrows at the quantity.

"Her teeth never stop growing," Luca said. "She needs things to chew on."

"Smart kid," she said, and slid Biscuit's carrier across the counter to him.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Wet oven mitts can burn your hands, because water in the cloth carries heat quickly and can turn to steam.
story:
Simon read the recipe card for the third time, mostly because it was written in his grandmother's handwriting and one line said "a modist amount of cinnamon," which raised questions. The card had arrived that morning in an envelope with a note: "Simon, you asked for my blueberry muffin recipe, so here it is. Bake them yourself, start to finish, and don't skip preheating the oven. Love, Gran." He had promised to report back by text.

He decided to eliminate every possible disaster before it started. Oven rack in the middle position. Flour measured by spooning it into the cup instead of scooping, because Gran's note had underlined that twice. He set the oven to preheat and heard it click and hum, which felt like a small victory. Then Lilah and Drayden knocked on the door, because he had invited them over to be, as he put it, "witnesses to history."

"You're witnesses, and also taste testers," Simon said. "But I do all the steps."

"Fine," said Drayden, "but if they're terrible, we're unanimous about it. All three of us saying so at once."

The batter came together lumpy and purple in a way the recipe apparently expected. While the muffins baked, Simon washed the mixing bowls, splashing water everywhere, including onto the oven mitt hanging on the hook by the sink. He didn't notice. Twenty-two minutes later the timer rang, and he grabbed the damp mitt and reached for the oven door.

"Stop!" Lilah yanked his arm back. "That mitt's soaked. Wet oven mitts can burn your hands. The water in the cloth carries heat really fast, and it can turn to steam."

"Steam?" Simon looked at the mitt, then at his own hand, which suddenly felt lucky. "So it's not just hot, it's like the water grabs the heat and charges it at me."

"Basically," Lilah said. "It's why you dry a mitt before you use it."

Drayden fetched the dry towel from the hook by the fridge, and Simon used that instead, folded double, to slide the tray out onto the cooling rack. The muffins were golden and lopsided and smelled like a bakery that had won an argument with a lesser bakery. They each took one, unanimous in their verdict of "not terrible, actually amazing," and Simon texted Gran a photo.

Her reply came fast: "Lopsided on the left, perfect on the right. So are mine. Welcome to the family recipe, Simon."

He set the phone down, picked up the last warm muffin, and broke it open so the steam rose between them.

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Feeling homesick while away from home is very common; nearly everyone misses something about home when they are away.
story:
Hunter had allocated the contents of his backpack with military care: sleeping bag rolled tight, toothbrush, two comics, and the small yellow flashlight he used at home for reading under the covers. His mom drove him to Bronson's house, and by nine o'clock they were deep into a game where Bronson had a total monopoly on the good properties and Hunter kept landing on them anyway. It was the best evening he'd had in weeks.

But at eleven, lying on the air mattress beside Bronson's bed in a room with opaque curtains that shut out even the streetlight, Hunter stared into the dark and felt something heavy settle in his chest. He missed his own ceiling, the one with the glow stars he'd arranged himself. He missed the sound of the kitchen tap his dad always forgot to turn off fully. He wondered, staring up at nothing, whether something was wrong with him. Then he thought about Elodie, who had gone to science camp last spring, and how she had come back telling everyone it was great, but her first week, she had called home twice in one night.

He decided to run a test, quiet and simple. "Bronson," he whispered. "You ever get homesick?"

There was a long pause, long enough that Hunter regretted asking. Then Bronson's voice came out of the dark, smaller than usual. "At my cousin's place in the summer. Every night, basically. I thought I was the only one."

"Elodie said it happens to almost everybody," Hunter said. "At camp she missed her cat so much she cried, and she said nearly everyone there missed something about home."

"Even the loud kids?"

"Even them."

Bronson was quiet again, but the air in the room felt different now, lighter, like a window had cracked open somewhere. Hunter clicked on the yellow flashlight and held it up so its beam made a small yellow circle on the strange ceiling.

"Wanna read comics till we fall asleep?"

"Pass me the one with the robots," Bronson said, and his hand appeared over the edge of the bed, waiting.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Tearing paper is a physical change even though it cannot be undone, because every torn piece is still paper.
story:
Jackson stood at the kitchen counter with three things lined up in front of him: an ice cube on a saucer, a steel nail, and a sheet of paper. Mr. Nair had said the quiz on Monday would ask them to sort changes into two groups, physical and chemical, and Jackson wanted to be ready. The ice cube was already sweating into a puddle, which seemed easy. Melting had to be physical. The nail was harder. It was just a nail from the garage, dull and grey, and nothing seemed to be happening to it at all.

Estelle had claimed the whole back porch for her experiment, which their parents prohibited anyone else from touching, because she was growing lichen in a jar and apparently lichen hated being moved. Jackson thought that was a strange science project, but Estelle could be strange in a useful way. She was the one who kept insisting that anything you could not undo had to be a chemical change. "You can't unburn toast," she had said on the bus that morning, "and you can't unrust a bike chain. Same thing. Can't undo it means chemical."

Jackson picked up the paper. He remembered Tuesday, when Graham had accidentally torn his worksheet reaching for a pencil, and Mr. Nair had told him to tape it. Graham had taped it and the tape had held, but the torn edge was still there, jagged and obvious, and the homework had still been accepted. That was the moment the thought started. Graham could not undo the tear. Nobody could. But the paper had not turned into something else, and nothing had felt hot or smelled strange. Every piece of the torn worksheet was still paper.

He tore the sheet in half, and the sound was smaller than he expected. He tore one half again, and again, until he had a scatter of small pieces across the counter. He picked one up. Paper. He picked up another. Paper. He could not put them back together, and he knew it, and yet nothing had become anything other than what it already was. He carried a fistful of pieces out to the porch, holding his other hand flat behind them so none would blow into the lichen jar.

"Estelle. You can't undo this, right?" He opened his hand. "But it's still paper. Every single piece."

Estelle set down her spray bottle and frowned at the pieces. "That's not fair. That breaks my whole rule."

"That's the point," Jackson said. He tilted his hand and let the bits of paper drift onto the porch boards between them, white scraps on grey wood.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink, which is why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off.
story:
Sebastian stood at the edge of the soccer field with his right arm in a cast, watching Arthur attempt an extravagant celebration every time he scored, spinning like a top and falling over in the grass. "One day you'll do that with me again," Arthur called. Sebastian raised the cast in salute, but what he was really thinking about was something Ms. Virtanen had said on the sidelines last week. She had mentioned, almost to herself, that a limb kept still in a cast loses muscle and gets thinner, and that it's obvious when the cast comes off. A hidden change, happening invisibly under the plaster. He wanted to test it.

He remembered the day of the break, four weeks ago. Izaiah had lobbed the ball high, Sebastian had sprinted for it, and then the ground came up to meet him in a way grounds are not supposed to. He could still hear the coach say, "That's the arm, folks," with terrible calm, as if announcing a substitute.

Now he had a theory. If stillness made the arm shrink, then moving it, even a little, might keep the muscle awake. He couldn't move the wrist or elbow, but his fingers stuck out of the cast, and his shoulder was free. So every evening while his mom cooked dinner, Sebastian gripped a tennis ball and squeezed it fifty times, then rolled his shoulder in slow circles. "What are you doing?" Izaiah asked once, watching him squeeze the ball during a game. "Experimenting," Sebastian said. Izaiah, who badly wanted to be named captain and had been doing extra laps all month to prove himself, nodded as if this were a reasonable kind of training.

The day the cast came off, Sebastian held both arms out side by side. The right one was thinner than the left, pale and strange, exactly the kind of change Ms. Virtanen had described. But when he gripped Izaiah's hand for an arm-wrestle on the bench, his arm didn't fold instantly. It held, trembling, for ten whole seconds. "Not bad for a ghost arm," Izaiah said, straining. "Half the team thinks you'll resign from soccer forever." Sebastian laughed and pushed harder. "Watch the shoulder," he said, and rolled it forward like a wheel.

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: On a coordinate grid, the horizontal number line is the x-axis and the vertical number line is the y-axis, and they cross at the origin, the point (0, 0).
story:
Math club met in the library on Tuesdays, at the table closest to the biography shelf, and this Tuesday Nicholas had one job: graph the equation y = 2x + 1 before the meeting ended. Ms. Fischer had handed out coordinate grids at the door and said whoever finished first got the last oatmeal cookie. Nicholas wanted that cookie more than he had wanted most things that week.

He solved the equation first, easy enough, and got his points: when x was zero, y was one; when x was one, y was three. Then he stared at the blank grid. It reminded him of the crossword his grandfather had shown him last summer, empty squares waiting for exactly the right answers in exactly the right places. Except a crossword told you where things went. This thing just sat there.

Across the table, Ivan was already plotting points, fast and confident, which should have been a warning. Emmeline leaned over, looked at Ivan's paper, and burst out laughing. "Your line is sideways," she said.

Ivan frowned at his graph. It went straight up the page instead of slanting across it, like a plant growing toward the ceiling. "The equation is right," he insisted. "I checked twice."

Nicholas looked at his own grid, then at Ivan's, and noticed something. Ivan had written his numbers along the vertical line and his other numbers along the horizontal one. Nicholas thought of the elevator in his aunt's building, how the numbers went up and down, never sideways. "Wait," he said slowly. "The horizontal one has to be the x-axis. That's where the x numbers go. The vertical one is the y-axis."

"Like elevator numbers," Emmeline said.

"And they cross in the middle, at zero, zero," Nicholas went on. "Ms. Fischer called it the origin. If you switch them, everything flips."

Ivan erased his axes and started over, muttering that his answer had at least been an approximate cousin of the right one. Nicholas plotted his own two points carefully, protecting them with his arm like he could insulate them from Ivan's mistakes, and drew the line through them.

It slanted exactly the way a line should. He raised his hand. "Ms. Fischer? I believe this cookie has an appointment with me."

"First rule of math club," Ivan said, still erasing. "Nobody tells Ivan his axes are backwards until after he's proud of himself."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Demand for necessities, such as essential medicines, changes little when their price changes; economists call this inelastic demand.
story:
Leo refreshed the marketplace page for the fourth time that evening. The price of the allergy inhaler his little sister needed had jumped from eighteen dollars to forty-two in one week, and every single listing still showed "only 3 left" or "selling fast." He had saved his allowance for a new skateboard deck, the lush green one with the dragon on it, but that money was going to have to wait.

At school the next morning he showed his phone to Kylie under the lunch table. "Look at this. The inhaler costs more than double now, but the sellers say they're selling out anyway. Why would anybody keep buying it?" Kylie scrolled through the listings. "Would your mom stop buying gas if gas cost double?" she asked. "No, but that's different, everybody needs gas." "So maybe it's the same for the inhaler," she said. Leo frowned. That didn't seem fair, but it did seem true.

During free period he tried to replicate what he saw with the inhaler on something people didn't need. He picked rainbow shoelaces, raised nothing, and watched. When a seller dropped the laces from six dollars to two, the "sold" count jumped from four a day to ninety. When a game sticker went from one dollar to five, sales basically stopped. Cheap and plentiful meant cheap; wanted and scarce meant expensive. He wrote the pattern in his notebook: normal stuff bends when the price bends.

But the inhaler didn't bend at all. He found an old listing from a month ago at sixteen dollars, sales steady, two a day. Now at forty-two, still two a day. He worked out the percentage in his head, more than double the price, and not one fewer sale. He was still staring at his notebook when Ms. Chatterjee passed his desk on yard duty. "What's got you frowning?" she asked. He showed her the two columns of numbers. "Demand for necessities like essential medicines changes little when their price changes," she said. "Economists call it inelastic demand." Then she moved on to shoo a group off the fence.

Leo copied the words down carefully, because if he was going to argue with the marketplace sellers, he wanted to sound like he knew what he was talking about. That afternoon he and Kylie found the same inhaler listed by a pharmacy three towns over, still at nineteen dollars, and he ordered it before the price there could change too. "One left in stock," Kylie read off the confirmation screen. "You beat it."

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In R. J. Palacio's novel Wonder, published in 2012, the teacher Mr. Browne gives the precept "When given the choice between being right or being kind, choose kind."
story:
Carson had read Wonder by R. J. Palacio all the way through, twice, and he still could not say what the theme was. That was the problem. Mr. Toussaint, the librarian, had promised the first team to finish its poster could present it at the assembly on Friday, and the poster needed a theme plus one quotation that proved it. Zane had already claimed the theme was friendship, which felt wrong to Carson but he could not say why.

He spread his notes across the table in the corner by the biography shelves. Zane kept finding quotes about Auggie making friends, but every time Carson read one, something nagged at him. The friends were not the point. Something invisible was underneath the story, like a rule the whole book obeyed without saying so. He had a test idea: if a theme was real, it should explain the big moments, especially the climax on the class trip, when the boys stood up for Auggie. Friendship explained that scene. But it did not explain why Summer sat with Auggie on the first day, before she even liked him.

Carson flipped pages, hunting. It would not be vain to check the chapter where the teacher, Mr. Browne, wrote a saying on the board, because he remembered something odd living there. He found it in September's section: "When given the choice between being right or being kind, choose kind." That was it. That line explained everything, even the parts about friendship.

"Zane," he said. "Mr. Browne calls that a precept. It's like a rule for how to live." Zane frowned at the page, then at his own poster, where a boy was being slammed out of the picture by kids who boycotted him for a whole year, the Year of Auggie's face on everyone's lips and nobody's kindness.

"So friendship is just the result," Zane said slowly. "Kindness is the cause."

"Test it," Carson said, and slid the book across the table. Zane read the line once more, then turned the poster over to its blank side and wrote one word at the top: CHOOSE KIND.

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: The site: operator limits a search to one website or domain ending, so adding site:.gov shows only pages from US government websites.
story:
Clara's class had twenty minutes of computer time, and she had one job: find out whether the storm rumors were true. Everyone on the bus had said a flood warning was posted for Friday, but nobody could say where they had read it. Lance swore it was on a website called StormFacts247, which sounded official to Clara until she opened it and found flashing banners promising a free weather app if she clicked a spinning prize wheel.

"There's a real warning somewhere," Carmen said, leaning over from the next computer. "My mom got an alert on her phone."

Clara typed flood warning Friday into the search bar and got a wall of results. The top three were ads, marked in tiny gray letters, and below those came blog posts full of exclamation points. Somewhere in the middle was an actual page from the National Weather Service, but it was buried so deep she almost missed it. She clicked it, read it, and frowned. No flood warning at all, at least not for their county.

She was about to resign herself to telling the bus that nobody knew anything when she noticed the address of the good page. It ended in .gov. She looked back at the junk sites. None of them ended that way. Slowly, she deleted her search and typed flood warning site:.gov. The results changed instantly. Every single one was a government page, no ads, no prize wheels, no blogs.

"Try that," she whispered to Carmen, pointing at her screen. "It's called the site operator. You just add site:.gov and it only shows government pages."

Carmen typed it, scrolled, and gasped. "Look. Severe thunderstorm watch, Thursday night. Not a flood."

Clara copied the warning onto her worksheet just as Ms. Hoffmann walked past and paused at her screen. "Now that," Ms. Hoffmann said, "is a real result."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Islam excuses people who are sick or travelling from the Ramadan fast, and they make up the missed days later.
story:
Eve woke up on the fourteenth morning of Ramadan with a sore throat and a thermometer reading of 38.6. Her mother felt her forehead, gave her water and medicine, and said no fasting today. Eve pulled the blanket up to her chin. Fourteen days she had managed, waking before dawn, skipping lunch while the smell of the cafeteria pizza drifted past. Now one fever was going to break her record.

"It doesn't break anything," her mother said from the doorway. "Sick people and travellers are excused from the fast. You make up the missed days later, after the month is over." She set a bowl of soup on the desk and went to call the school.

Eve ate the soup, but she kept thinking about it. It sounded like a loophole, and loopholes bothered her. She got her phone and texted Vicky, who was fasting with her family across the street. Does ur mom say sick ppl dont have to fast?? Vicky wrote back: yes, and travelers too, they do the days after Eid. Eve stared at the screen. Two different mothers, the same rule.

She decided to test it on her grandmother, who had fasted every Ramadan since before Eve was born. On the video call, Eve asked, "If I'm sick on a fasting day, what happens?" Her grandmother held up one crooked finger. "You are excused. When you are well, you fast that day another time." Eve asked how many days she would owe. "One day for each day you miss," her grandmother said. "Write it on your calendar so you don't forget." Eve wrote it: 1 day, in pencil, after Eid.

The fever was infectious, in a way; her little brother caught it two days later and lay on the couch groaning about missing his first-ever half-day fast. Eve sat beside him with the thermometer. "You're excused," she told him. "Sick and travelling, both excused, you make it up later. Even grown-ups do." He asked whether watching three episodes of a show counted as travelling. She said no.

That evening their father did the arithmetic out loud at dinner. If a percentage of the month's days were missed, the calendar just stretched a bit longer, that was all. Eve looked at the pencilled note on the calendar and then at the window, where the sun was going down and her mother was pouring tea. Fourteen days done, one owed, and the month still had room in it. She turned the pencil over and wrote beneath the first note: Day 15, insha'Allah.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: A fair coin toss gives each side an equal chance, which is why sports such as American football and cricket use a coin toss to decide how a game starts.
story:
The argument started before the game did. Fatima's team wanted first kick because Fatima had brought the ball, and Edison's team wanted it because Edison had chosen the captains in the first place. Behind them, Mr. Walker called from the picnic table that the cake was coming out in ten minutes, so whatever they were going to play, they had to play it fast. The sprinklers had left the grass so saturated that every footstep made a squelching sound, and the party guests were drifting away toward the food table one by one.

"Here's the actual problem," Victoria said, stepping between them. "Both teams want to go first, and there's only one first. That's it. That's the whole fight." Edison opened his mouth, then shut it, because she was right. Fatima crossed her arms but nodded.

Victoria pulled a quarter out of her sweatshirt pocket. "A fair coin toss gives each side an equal chance. That's why American football and cricket use a coin toss to decide how a game starts." She had learned that from her older brother last season, and she figured if it settled games played in giant stadiums, it could settle a birthday party. She flipped the coin five times to show them: two heads, then a tail, then two more heads, landing differently enough that nobody could call it rigged. "So here's the rule. Fatima calls it in the air, and nobody argues after. That's fair for both teams, and it's fair every time we play."

"Fine," said Fatima. "But I get to call it, since it was my ball." Edison looked at the shrinking group of guests, then at the cake candles Mr. Walker was counting out loud, and shrugged. "Heads," Fatima said, the moment the coin spun up.

It came down tails. Edison's team jogged onto the wet grass, and Fatima, muttering that Victoria would make an exceptional diplomat someday, ran to grab her position just as Mr. Walker lit the first candle.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, where bones lengthen during childhood; a break through a growth plate can affect how the bone grows.
story:
Theodore sat in the emergency room with his right arm propped on a pillow, and it throbbed every time the nurse's cart rattled past. Two hours earlier he had been on the monkey bars at the park, showing Adnan and Nolan that he could skip the fourth bar entirely. He had skipped it. He had also skipped the fifth, the sixth, and the ground came up much faster than his plan allowed for. Adnan had sprinted home for help, Nolan had stayed and told him a story about his uncle's broken leg to keep him from crying, and now here they all were, waiting for the doctor to come back with his x-ray.

"You want the good news or the weird news first?" the doctor asked, holding up the film against the light. Theodore asked for the weird news, because obviously. "Your break is right here," she said, tapping a spot on the long bone of his forearm, "and near the ends of long bones are growth plates, made of cartilage, where bones lengthen while you're still growing." Theodore squinted at the ghostly grey picture. He could see the crack, a thin dark line like a hair in old paint, but the end of the bone just looked like bone to him. How could she possibly know where cartilage was if cartilage didn't even show up on an x-ray? He asked her that, and she smiled and said that was exactly the right question.

"Cartilage looks darker on the film," she said. "See that band near the end? That's the growth plate. Your crack stops short of it." She drew an invisible line with her fingertip, and Theodore leaned closer, testing her idea against what he could see. The dark band sat between the end of the bone and the crack, like a fence the crack had failed to climb. So the good news, he worked out, was that his break missed it. He asked why that mattered so much, and she said that a break through a growth plate can affect how the bone grows. Theodore nodded slowly, thinking about his arm being one length forever while the other one kept going, like wearing one short sock for the rest of his life.

"Credible?" said Nolan from the chair by the door. "You've got a broken arm and you're interrogating the doctor." "I'm gathering facts," Theodore said. The doctor laughed and said his questions were better than most she got from adults, and that kids with questions like that tended to thrive in hospitals, in the sense of escaping them quickly. She said the arm would need good blood flow to heal, since blood vessels carry the stuff bones use to repair themselves, and that the cast would hold everything steady while that happened. The plaster was warm and heavy as she wrapped it. When it dried, Theodore wrote his name on it in careful letters, and then, below that, DO NOT SKIP THE FOURTH BAR. Adnan shook his head. "You're going to try it again, aren't you." "Monday," Theodore said.

activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
knowledge_domain: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
fact: A monologue is a long speech by one character, spoken to other characters on stage or to the audience.
story:
The porch boards at Grandpa's house were warm under Nathan's sneakers, and the screen door banged behind him as he carried his script outside. He had three days before drama camp auditions, and he still sounded like a kid reading a grocery list. The monologue he'd chosen belonged to a sailor who thought he'd lost his brother at sea, and every time Nathan ran it, the words came out fast and flat, one after another, like he couldn't wait to be finished.

He tried it again, louder this time, and startled a sparrow off the railing. "There was a storm," he recited, "and in the storm I lost him." Then he plowed straight into the next line, and the next, until Hassan's voice came from the side of the yard, where Hassan had arrived on his bike without Nathan noticing. "Who are you talking to? There's nobody out here."

"That's the thing," Nathan said, lowering the script. "I thought a monologue meant talking to yourself, so I've been doing it like a crazy person on a porch." Hassan shook his head. "Mr. Whitehead said it's a long speech by one character, spoken to other characters on stage or to the audience. You're supposed to be talking to somebody. That's the whole point." Nathan stared at the empty yard, then at the porch railing, then at Hassan himself, and something rearranged itself in his head. He wasn't talking to nobody. He was talking to someone who wasn't there yet, and his job was to make the audience believe the person existed.

He formulated a plan on the spot: pick a spot in the hedge for the imaginary listener, and aim every line at it. The first component was the pause. He slowed down, let the silence sit after "I lost him," and pressed one hand flat against his chest the way his grandfather did when he talked about Grandma. The second run-through felt less tedious and more like weather changing. His voice dropped low on the sad lines and rose on the angry ones, and when he finished, Hassan clapped twice against his knee.

"Do it one more time," Hassan said, settling onto the porch step. "Do it like he's really standing in the hedge." Nathan lifted his script, took a breath, and looked straight at the dark leaves at the end of the yard. "There was a storm," he began.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A tomato is botanically a fruit, but in 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled in Nix v. Hedden that it counted as a vegetable for import taxes.
story:
Eli crouched between the rows of his vegetable garden at Hollow Creek Farm, counting tomato seedlings. He had spent his whole spring budget on seeds, soil, and twoeccentric metal cages that Mr. Pérez swore kept raccoons away, and now the first green tomatoes hung like small lanterns. His plan was simple: sell the extras at the farm's roadside stand and earn enough for the mountain bike in the shop window in town. But when he lugged his first basket of ripe tomatoes to the stand, Londyn was already there behind the table, arms crossed.

"Those go on the fruit shelf," she said. "My aunt charges fruit prices, and fruit is cheaper by the pound."

"They're vegetables," Eli said. "I planted a vegetable garden. Everyone knows that."

Jiya, sorting peppers beside them, grinned. "It's both. Sort of." She pulled out the farm's little reference book and flipped to a marked page. "Botanically a tomato is a fruit. But in 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled in Nix v. Hedden that it counted as a vegetable for import taxes." She tapped the page. "So the tax people called it a vegetable, even though the science calls it a fruit."

Eli frowned. That did not seem like a real answer. Two names for one tomato, depending on who was asking? He thought about it while he stacked his basket. It was like the word "budget," which meant one thing in his math homework and another in his mother's kitchen. The meaning changed with the context. So Londyn's aunt could charge whatever price her stand used, and no one could argue with science alone. Eli proposed a test: put half his tomatoes on the vegetable shelf at vegetable prices, half on the fruit shelf at fruit prices, and see which sold out first. Londyn agreed, mostly because she wanted to be right.

By closing time, both halves had sold. The vegetable shelf went first, but only by ten minutes. Londyn counted out Eli's earnings, and Jiya wrote a new sign for the stand: TOMATOES, YES. Eli folded the money into his pocket and looked down the road toward town. "Two more baskets," he said, "and the bike is mine."

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: A password manager creates a different random password for every site and locks them all behind one master password, so a person only has to remember one.
story:
Anders's grandmother kept every password in a spiral notebook beside the desktop computer, and today she could not find the one for the grocery store's website. "It has to be here," she kept saying, flipping pages with names like FLOWERS2 and catcatcat. Sydney leaned over the desk while Anders pulled up a chair beside her.

"You use catcatcat for the grocery store too," Sydney said, pointing at a line halfway down the page. "And for the library. And, wow, for the bank."

"So?" Anders said. "It's easy to remember."

Sydney chewed her lip. She had read something about this, and now a possibility was taking shape, one she couldn't see directly but could test. "Think of it like this. If somebody finds out catcatcat works at the grocery store, they'll try it at the bank next. Every place that shares it is connected, even though nobody can see the connection." She looked at the notebook, where the same few passwords revolved from page to page like planets on the same orbit.

"That's not plausible," Anders said. "Who would bother?"

"Let's ask your grandma about the weird emails she got last month," Sydney said. Grandma admitted that yes, she had clicked on a coupon link, and yes, the bank had called about a charge for a mortgage payment she never made. Anders went pale. "Okay. Okay, that's plausible."

Sydney took out her phone. "There's a thing called a password manager," she said, showing them an app her mom used. "It makes a different random password for every site and locks them all behind one master password. So you only have to remember one." Grandma peered at the screen. "One? I can remember one."

They spent the evening setting it up. Sydney let the app generate passwords full of nonsense like 7vQ$mz, and Grandma wrote the single master password on one card for her wallet. Anders fed them crackers and announced each new password like a game show host. "The bank gets... Xk9tqr! A stunning victory for randomness!"

When they finished, Grandma closed the notebook, held it up, and dropped it in the recycling bin. "Goodbye, catcatcat," Anders said solemnly. "You served us poorly."

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Sleepwalking is more common in children than in adults, and most children who sleepwalk outgrow it.
story:
Emily had been waiting for this sleepover all week, and now she was standing in Everlee's bedroom holding her backpack like it was full of treasure. In a way, it was: a bag of sour candy, a deck of cards, and her debate notes for Monday, which she and Marika had promised to run through before they slept.

"Quiz me while we set up the fort," Emily said, dumping blankets onto the floor between the beds. "I have to be eloquent for Ms. García or my team loses the tariff round to the eighth graders."

Everlee grabbed a pillow and lobbed it at her. "Later. Fort first, debate second, candy always." Marika laughed so hard she snorted, and the three of them draped a quilt over two chair backs until the whole corner of the room glowed with string lights.

Emily woke past midnight to a soft thump. Everlee was out of bed, eyes open, walking straight toward the door with slow, shuffling steps. Marika sat up, frozen. Emily's heart pounded, but she remembered her little brother doing exactly this last summer, and her mom saying the words that now steadied her: "Sleepwalking is more common in children than in adults, and most children outgrow it." Nothing was wrong. Everlee wasn't awake, and you weren't supposed to shake a sleepwalker.

"Just guide her back," Emily whispered. "Watch."

She took Everlee's shoulders gently and turned her around, steering her step by step until Everlee folded back into bed like nothing had happened. In the dark, Marika let out a huge breath.

"Okay," Marika whispered, "I thought a ghost. I officially retract the ghost." She had spent the whole evening insisting the house was haunted, and now she changed her mind on the spot. "That was the coolest, creepiest thing I've ever seen."

Emily climbed into her own blanket, grinning into the dark. "Tomorrow you're helping me argue tariffs, and I will be eloquent."

"Deal," Marika whispered. "Night, ghost girl."

"Night," Emily said, and popped one last sour candy into her mouth.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: A kneaded eraser can be pressed and shaped to lift graphite off the paper, which lets an artist pull a highlight back out of shading.
story:
Maeva sat at the kitchen table with her sketchbook open to a circle she had turned into a sphere, at least she hoped so. Mr. Mori had shown the class a photo of a plaster ball under one lamp, with a bright spot, a dark side, and a shadow spilling onto the table. "You have to convey where the light is coming from," he had said, "or the sphere looks flat." Maeva wanted her drawing to look so round that Andie would swear she could pick it up off the page.

She shaded and shaded, pressing harder on the side away from the light. Then she sat back and groaned. Her graphite had crept right over the highlight, the brightest spot, until it was the same grey as everything around it. The sphere looked like a dusty moon. She almost flipped to a fresh page.

Instead she pulled the gray lump out of her pencil case, the squishy eraser that felt like dough. She had only ever rubbed erasers back and forth, which smeared graphite as often as it removed it. But this one was different. She squeezed it into a pointy shape, pressed the point straight down onto the brightest spot of her sphere, and lifted it away. When she peeled the eraser off, a pale patch had come with it. The graphite had sunk into the soft, shapeable eraser instead of staying on the paper. "Emy-Jade, look!" she yelled toward the phone propped against the sugar bowl. "It lifts it off! You press and it takes the pencil with it!"

"That's actually so good," Emy-Jade said from the screen. "I thought you'd have to start over." She had told Maeva an hour ago that the drawing was probably ruined and she should just trace a real orange instead. "Okay, I change my mind. Don't start over. Do the highlight thing on mine too, tomorrow at school?"

"Deal." Maeva pressed the eraser down again and again, dabbing the highlight back out of her shading, then checked the left and right sides against each other for symmetry so the shadow wouldn't look crooked. On the table in front of the sphere she drew the cast shadow, darkest right under the ball, and made it stretch away from the light like something predatory creeping across the floor.

She held the sketchbook at arm's length, turning it toward the window. The sphere glowed on one side and melted into shadow on the other, and she ran one finger through the air above it, circling the bright spot. "Pick me up," she whispered. "I dare you."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: A conductor shows the first beat of each bar, called the downbeat, with a downward movement of the hand or baton.
story:
Grandma's living room had been turned into a rehearsal hall, which meant the good chairs were shoved against the wall and Mr. Santos stood in front of the fireplace waving a pencil like it was a baton. "Once more from the top," he said. "Altos, you are the engine of this piece. Sopranos, try not to float away like balloons."

Kaitlyn was an alto, and proud of it, until the sopranos started. The moment Heaven and the other sopranos slid into their high line, Kaitlyn's ears betrayed her. Her notes crept upward to chase theirs, like a dog following the wrong scent. She'd open her mouth meaning to sing one thing and a completely different thing would come out, and Gibson, standing beside her, would grin without even looking at her.

"You climbed again," he whispered after they stopped. "Three whole steps. I counted."

"Thanks for the weather report," she whispered back, but she knew he was right. Worse, in the middle of the song she had lost count of the bars entirely, and when the altos had a rest she came back in two bars late, singing boldly and alone. Grandma, knitting in the corner by the humming generator that kept the lights on through the storm outage, had raised one eyebrow. Even the knitting seemed to disapprove.

During the break, Kaitlyn watched Mr. Santos instead of eating the biscuits Grandma carried in. Every time the group started again, his hand went down on the first beat of each bar, then up, down, up, like a slow-motion seesaw. She counted along silently, matching the falls to the pulse of the music. "Mr. Santos," she called, "that downward motion, is there a word for it?"

"That's the downbeat," he said, tapping his pencil against his knee. "First beat of every bar." Then he sipped his tea as if he hadn't just handed her a treasure map.

She had a theory, and like all good theories it needed testing. If the conductor's hand showed her where every bar began, then even if the sopranos pulled her ears off the road, she could find her place again just by watching, not listening. It sounded almost too easy to be credible, like a diet based on biscuits. But it was worth a try.

They sang the piece again, and sure enough Heaven's soaring line grabbed her on the fourth page, and her note wobbled, and she lost the bar count completely. Instead of panicking, she locked her eyes on the pencil. Down. One. Down. Two. When her entrance came she dropped back in exactly on time, and this time she held her part down where it belonged, steady as a fence post while the sopranos flew over the top. Gibson elbowed her at the end. "No climbing," he reported. "Zero steps." Grandma raised her teacup in salute, and Kaitlyn bowed.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Fossils are found almost only in sedimentary rock, because the heat that forms igneous and metamorphic rock usually destroys remains.
story:
Eva had spent all Saturday digging behind the garden shed, and her wagon held twenty-three rocks, every one of them a possible fossil. At least, she hoped so. She had found a rock with a ridged shape that looked exactly like a shell, and she was already imagining it in a museum case with a little card reading "Discovered by Eva."

She lugged the wagon across the yard to where Maxine sat on the porch steps, sorting a pile of gravel into paper cups. "Look!" Eva said, holding up the shell rock. "I think it's a fossil. I'm going to find ten more."

Maxine frowned at it. "Mr. Grewal told us fossils show up in sedimentary rock. That's rock made from layers of mud and sand piling up." She pointed at the shell rock's sparkly, banded surface. "Yours looks like the ones he called metamorphic, the kind that got squashed and cooked deep underground. And that one over there, with the bubbles in it like a sponge, is igneous. It came from cooled-off lava."

Eva's shoulders dropped, but only for a second. "Then I just have to sort them all," she said. "Into three piles. Sedimentary, metamorphic, igneous. The fossil hunt depends on it." She dumped the wagon out onto the grass, and the two of them got to work, with Zachary jogging over from next door to join in because anything involving piles and sorting was, in his opinion, voluntary and therefore worth doing.

Zachary grabbed the sponge rock and stacked it on the igneous pile. "Volcanoes are the best ones," he said. Eva picked up her shell rock again and turned it in the light, thinking hard. If Maxine was right, then fossils belonged almost only with the sedimentary rocks, because the heat that made the other two kinds usually destroyed any remains. "So the banded ones and the volcano ones are out," she said slowly. "No fossils hiding in those. The muddy, layered ones are the only ones worth cracking open."

She checked each rock against the rule, and when she found a dull gray stone with thin stripes like stacked pages, her heart started pounding. It fit the sedimentary pile perfectly. She carried it to the porch, tapped it gently with a hammer wrapped in a dish towel, and the stone split along one of its stripes. There, pressed into the flat face, was the perfect coil of an ancient shell.

"It worked!" Eva shouted, waving both halves over her head. "The rule worked!"

Zachary came running, and Maxine nearly knocked over the cups of gravel. "Okay," Eva said, already scanning the yard for dull gray stone. "The wagon's still half full. Sort first, crack second. Who's with me?"

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: A sleeping pad keeps someone warm in a tent because the cold ground pulls heat away from the body faster than the air does.
story:
Jade had never been to a sleepover before, so she packed like the night might last a week: two flashlights, three snacks, and a folded foam pad that her older cousin swore by. Edie's house had a basement rec room with a couch, a ping-pong table, and stairs that leveled off into a little plateau before the carpet began. But Edie's plan was bigger than the basement. "We're sleeping in the tent in the backyard," she announced. Zoelie, who had arrived first, was already dragging sleeping bags toward the door.

Out in the yard, Edie's little brother hovered near the tent, and his story about last summer was not coherent at all. He said he had frozen in that tent even though the night had been mild and he had a good sleeping bag rated for cold weather. Jade didn't believe him at first. Warm bag, mild air, how do you freeze? She lay down inside on the bare tent floor to test it, keeping her foam pad folded under only half of her body. Within minutes she knew he had been telling the truth. The half of her on the ground turned cold while the half on the pad stayed warm, which meant one thing: the ground itself was the problem, pulling heat out of her faster than the air did. The pad was the fix.

"Can we install the pads now?" she asked, and Mr. Foster laughed and helped them lay the foam out, two by the door, two in the back. Jade counted five sleepers and four pads, so she pushed hers toward Edie.

That was when the first fat raindrops hit the nylon. Mr. Foster poked his head in. "Storm's rolling in. Tent comes down, everyone moves to the rec room." The girls carried everything inside, and Zoelie flopped her sleeping bag straight onto the concrete by the couch. Jade shook her head and slid a pad under her. "Trust me," she said. "The floor down here is still the ground." Zoelie scooted onto the last pad, and the five of them lay in a row while the rain drummed on the narrow basement window. "Warmest sleepover ever," Edie whispered, and Jade clicked off her flashlight.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends, and once these plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller.
story:
Emile stood with his back against the doorframe in Amelya's kitchen while she drew a pencil line above his head. He had done the same thing at home that morning, and the morning before, and the line never moved. Rayyan had shot up four inches since summer, and Emile had grown exactly none, as far as he could tell.

"Maybe your ruler's wrong," Amelya said. She held the pencil flat against the top of his head again and made a second line. The two lines sat so close together they looked like one thick line.

"Rulers don't grow," Emile said. "I checked with the measuring tape too. Sixty-two and a quarter inches, same as Tuesday."

Rayyan leaned against the counter, eating cereal from the box. "My brother says it happens all at once. You go to bed one night and wake up huge."

Emile didn't believe that. He had woken up plenty of mornings and stayed the same height, so Rayyan's brother was either teasing or guessing. Something had to control it, some rule he couldn't see. He thought about Amelya's arm, which she had broken last winter.

"When you broke your arm," he said, "the doctor showed you your X-ray, right? Did he say anything about how bones grow?"

Amelya pulled up a photo on her tablet, the one of her own forearm in pale grey on black. "He said bones grow longer at the growth plates, near the ends. See those dark lines by my wrist? That's them. And once they close after puberty, you stop getting taller. He said my plates were wide open, so my arm would catch up."

Emile took the tablet and zoomed in on the dark lines. Growth plates near the ends of bones, and once they closed, that was it, finished. So growing had a limit built into the bone itself, like a door that shut behind you.

"So you can't tell from the outside whether they're open or closed," he said slowly. "But if I'm still sixty-two inches, my plates can't have closed, or I'd never have gotten this tall to begin with." He looked up. "The lines on your doorframe are too close together to show anything. Growth must be slower than one pencil line a day."

Amelya grinned and wiped the marks off with her thumb. "Then we measure once a month. And you should probably sleep more. My mom says the body prioritizes sleep when you're growing."

"Sleep is only one component," Emile said. "Rayyan's brother sleeps till noon and he's still short."

Rayyan put down the cereal box. "My brother is a chronic liar," he said. "He told me our dog could count."

Emile laughed and marked the date in his notebook: October ninth, sixty-two and a quarter inches. "Next measurement, November ninth," he said, and clicked the pen shut.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: A frost, hailstorm or drought that ruins part of a strawberry crop reduces the supply, which pushes the price of the remaining berries up.
story:
The strawberry cartons at the corner stand near school cost four dollars in June, and now, three weeks later, they cost seven. Sofia stood in front of the stand with her friend Susana, holding the last of her allowance, and wondered why. She needed an answer by tomorrow, because Mr. He had assigned each student a two-minute talk on why prices change, and she had picked strawberries on a whim.

"It's the frost," the stand owner said, counting change for another customer. "Late frost took out half the berries out west. What's left, everybody wants." He shrugged, as if that settled it, and turned to the next bin.

On the walk home, Sofia turned the words over like a stone in her pocket. Fewer berries, higher price. She suspected there was a rule hiding in there, something you couldn't see directly, the way you can't watch Earth orbit the sun but you can watch the seasons. She wanted a diagnosis of the price, not just a guess. That night she called Vivienne, whose family ran a fruit stand two streets over.

"Strawberries?" Vivienne said. "We're selling ours for seven dollars too. Last month it was four. My dad grumbles about the frost every single morning."

Sofia sat up. Two stands, same jump, same frost. But maybe she was being biased, she told herself, wanting the frost to be the answer just because she had heard it first. She needed another test. So the next morning before school, she tried a stand that sold apples instead, a block farther on. Apples: two dollars a basket, same price as in June. Whatever had happened had happened to strawberries, not to everything.

In Mr. He's class, Sofia stood at the front with a pint of berries she had finally bought, seven dollars lighter. "A late frost ruined part of the strawberry crop," she said. "That cut the supply. The berries that were left went up in price, from four dollars to seven. Apples weren't touched by the frost, so apples stayed the same."

Mr. He made a small checkmark on his clipboard. "And if next winter I want cheap strawberries?"

"Wait," said Susana from the second row, "and pray for no hail."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Puberty usually begins between ages 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys, and starting anywhere in that range is normal.
story:
Kaylee sat in the dentist's waiting room holding a pamphlet about flossing and not reading a single word. Her mom had a checkup first, which meant Kaylee had time to think, and the thing she kept thinking about was Edward's face in science class when Ms. Cho asked them to move to lab stations and the whole room had smelled like someone's forgotten gym socks. Her socks. She had worn her sneakers without socks three days in a row because it was easier, and now Elie had started sitting one seat over.

A flashback kept playing in her head: fourth grade, when she'd told everyone that deodorant was only for old people, because her grandpa kept a stick in his truck. Elie had laughed so hard she fell off the swings. Kaylee had been so certain then. Now she felt vulnerable in a way she couldn't have explained to fourth-grade Kaylee, like everyone could see a secret written on her.

The hygienist called her back, and while Kaylee lay in the chair with the little paper bib on, the dentist leaned in beside her. "Big teeth," he said. "Twelve-year molars coming along nicely. Growing fast lately?"

Kaylee nodded, then remembered she wasn't supposed to nod with tools in her mouth.

"You can talk when we pause," he said. "Anything on your mind? Sometimes patients my age have questions."

"I'm twelve," she said, "and nobody told me when any of this starts. Like the sweating. And Edward still looks exactly like a little kid and he's embarrassed about it. Is one of us weird?"

The dentist rinsed his tools. "Puberty usually begins between ages 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys," he said. "Starting anywhere in that range is normal. So you're both normal."

Kaylee did the math on the ceiling tiles while he checked her molars. Edward, at 12, was inside 9 to 14. She was inside 8 to 13. Nobody was early or late; she'd just assumed everyone should match up in the same grade, which, she realized, was a bias, like assuming the tallest kid was the oldest. Last month a kid a whole year younger had towered over Edward.

Afterward, in the waiting room, she pulled out her phone and texted Elie: "You know that thing I said about socks? I'm getting deodorant at the store. The kind that smells like rain."

Elie texted back a single thumbs-up, then: "rain?? get the coconut one."

At the drugstore Kaylee stood in the aisle for ten minutes, sniffing every stick, and finally bought both.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The American Camp Association was founded in 1910, under the name Camp Directors Association of America, to set common standards for organized camps.
story:
Sophia had until five o'clock to finish packing, because the camp bus left at six the next morning, and her duffel bag was still half empty on her bedroom floor. Travis sat on the rug, reading the camp brochure she'd gotten in the mail.

"There's a weird sign in this picture," he said, tapping the page. "By the gate. It says the camp is accredited by something called the American Camp Association."

Sophia knelt beside him. The sign in the photo showed a flame inside a circle. She wondered what a camp had to do to earn a sign like that, and who decided. It reminded her of the science fair in fourth grade, when she'd found a tiny green larva on her milkweed plant and kept a notebook for three weeks, watching it expose its skin and change shape day by day. She couldn't see inside the larva. She had to guess the rules from what happened outside. Maybe the sign worked the same way. If she could find out who put it there and why, she'd know something hidden about the camp itself.

She ran downstairs for her mom's laptop and typed the name into the search bar. The first result made her sit up straight. "Travis, look at this."

He leaned over her shoulder.

"The American Camp Association was founded in 1910," she read slowly, "under the name Camp Directors Association of America, to set common standards for organized camps." She said it again to herself. "So that's the rule. The sign means the camp followed standards, and it's been happening since 1910."

"Standards like what?"

"Like, is the water safe? Do the counselors know first aid?" She spun the laptop toward him. "It's a hundred years of people checking."

Travis grinned. "Then your week is going to be way better than mine. I'm stuck at home with my little brother, and his laugh is infectious. He gets everyone going."

Sophia rolled a sweatshirt into a tight cylinder and wedged it into the duffel. Outside, the sky over the rooftops had turned the color of a peach, and somewhere down the block a screen door banged twice. She looked at the flame inside its circle on the brochure, then folded the page and slipped it into her jacket pocket, so she could compare the picture to the real gate the moment the bus pulled in.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Wet snow near the freezing point packs into snowballs well because it holds a thin layer of liquid water, while very cold, dry snow crumbles.
story:
The snow had come down all night, and by morning the school's website said what Anais had hoped: classes were prohibited for the day. She was out the door before her mother finished saying the word breakfast.

Roland and Maelys were already on the corner, stomping a path through knee-deep drifts. "Snowman," Roland announced, as if it had already been decided. "Biggest one on the street."

It was decided, and it was a disaster. Anais scooped a mound of snow and pressed it between her gloves, but the snow fell apart like sugar. She tried again, packing harder, and it crumbled through her fingers. Maelys laughed, then tried herself, then stopped laughing. "It's powder," she said. "It just won't stick."

Anais sat back on her heels and looked at the stuff closely. Back in November, before the deep cold, she remembered the first snowfall of the year. She and her cousin had thrown snowballs that held together so well they left marks on the fence. That snow had almost felt damp. This snow was different, dry as sand, more like something from an arid desert than from a cloud. The memory gave her an idea: the two snows weren't the same stuff at all, and something had changed between them.

She held out a fistful to Roland. "Squeeze it." He squeezed. Nothing. "Now squeeze your mitten." He pressed his wool mitten and a few flakes clung to the fibers. "It doesn't even stick to your glove," Anais said. "It's too dry to hold anything."

"So we can't build a snowman," Roland said. "The whole snow day is ruined."

"No. We wait." Anais pointed at the sky, where the sun was climbing behind a thin haze. The air had warmed almost to freezing overnight, and the drifts on the sunny side of the street had already gone from sparkling white to a duller, denser look. She figured the afternoon would soften the top layer, the way it had in November.

They waited by sledding on the hill behind Ms. Sutherland's hedge until their mittens were soaked through. Then Anais walked back to the sunny drift, scooped, and pressed. The snow gathered into a ball with barely any effort, a little damp against her gloves, holding its shape when she turned it over.

"I told you," she said, and rolled the ball along the sidewalk until it grew too heavy to push.

Maelys grabbed a handful and threw the first snowball of the afternoon. It hit Roland square in the shoulder and stuck.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta.
story:
The food bank took up the common room of the seniors' residence every second Saturday, and on Zoe's first morning she was handed a clipboard and a crate of dented cans. Asha was already sorting pasta by shape, which struck Zoe as ambitious, and Cooper was reading labels aloud in a dramatic voice, "Peach nectar, again," as though the crate were full of treasure.

Zoe's job was the shelf at the back. She noticed something odd within half an hour: the tins of sardines never moved. Neither did the hot sauce. But the peach nectar, the pudding cups, and the soft bread vanished by noon. She formed a theory. If most of the people who used this food bank lived here, in the residence, then maybe the food that went fast was food that was easy to chew, and the food that stayed was not. It was a rule she couldn't see directly, only its results, like footprints in snow.

"Excuse me," she said to a small woman examining a jar of chili flakes. "Do you ever take the sardines?"

The woman looked at her with great patience. "Do I look like I have all my teeth?"

Zoe anticipated the answer would be no, and it was. She moved the sardines to the bottom shelf and put the pudding cups at eye level. By the end of the morning, the pudding was gone and the sardines remained, which felt like proof, though a quiet kind.

Later, the woman wandered back with a box of crackers. "You're new," she said. "How long have food banks even existed in this country?"

Zoe had only a vague idea, so she guessed, "A hundred years?"

The woman snorted so hard that Cooper looked up from the pasta. "Canada's first food bank opened in 1981, in Edmonton, Alberta. I read it on the poster by the door. Twice."

Zoe checked the poster. It was true, printed right there under a drawing of a shopping cart. She wrote it on her clipboard in case anyone else asked.

Asha held up a can of soup. "Soft or chewy?"

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In S. E. Hinton's The Outsiders, published in 1967, Johnny's dying message to Ponyboy is to "stay gold," meaning to hold on to his goodness and innocence.
story:
Marcus had one page of notes and zero ideas, which was, he figured, a ratio that had never once earned an A. Mr. Takahashi's assignment sat in the middle of the library table like a dare: find the theme of your novel and prove it with one quotation. Marcus had chosen The Outsiders because everyone said it was good, and now everyone was apparently wrong about it being easy.

"Theme is the big idea underneath," Tyler said, chewing his pencil. "Like the moral." He was writing about a book where a dog gets lost, so his theme was "dogs get lost," and he seemed at peace with that.

"It's not a moral," said Grayden, who had finished already and was now supervising the other two with the patience of a lifeguard at an empty pool. "It has to cover the whole book. One quotation. From the actual pages."

Marcus flipped through his copy. The book was published in 1967, said the page at the front, by S. E. Hinton, which he'd assumed was a man and was wrong about. There were fights and a church fire and a lot of hair product. Any of those could be the theme, probably. Hair product, definitely.

Then he stopped at the letter. Johnny, dying, had written a message to Ponyboy, and near the end of it were two words: "stay gold." Marcus read them, then read the sentence before them, then read the whole letter again, slower, because something was clicking the way a combination lock clicks when you're not even trying. Johnny wasn't talking about treasure. He was telling Ponyboy to hold on to his goodness and innocence, the way gold is the thing that stays bright while everything else tarnishes. Two words in one letter, and suddenly the fights and the fire and even the hair product all pointed the same direction. The whole novel was about keeping what's good in you when the world tries to grind it off.

"Found it," Marcus said. He was agile about getting his notebook open, which was more energy than he'd shown all week.

"Found what?" Tyler asked.

"The theme. Two words." Marcus wrote them down and underlined them, once, twice, then a third time for luck. "Stay gold."

Grayden leaned over. "That works. That actually works."

Mr. Takahashi passed by their table, paused, and read the notebook upside down, which teachers can apparently do. "Nice," he said. "Page number?"

"178," Marcus said, already flipping to it.

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: In the equation y = mx + b, the number b is the y-intercept, the point where the line crosses the y-axis.
story:
Vincent sat at the kitchen table with a pencil, graph paper, and his math worksheet, which had one problem circled twice in red: Graph y = 2x + 5. He had solved two-step equations all week, getting x alone one step at a time, but the graphing part made his stomach knot up. He wanted to get it before Friday's quiz, because Ms. Gupta had promised the class they could graph a real phone plan when they finished, and Marika had already said she was on problem ten.

His mom set down a plate of crackers and peeked at the paper. "That looks like a rocket trajectory," she said.

"It's supposed to be a line," Vincent said. "But I don't know where it starts." He had made a table of values, plugging in 1, 2, and 3 for x, and the points climbed upward like stairs. Somewhere below the stairs, the line had to begin, but his table stopped before he found it. He decided to test the smallest number he could think of: zero.

He substituted 0 for x, and the equation became y = 2 times 0 plus 5, which was just 5. He plotted the point (0, 5), and there it was, sitting exactly on the y-axis, the tall vertical line down the middle of the grid. He checked his staircase points again, and every one lined up in a straight slant through that single dot. "The plus five is where it starts," he said out loud. He remembered Ms. Gupta calling that spot the y-intercept, the point where the line crosses the y-axis. He drew the line in one careful stroke and it looked authentic, like the ones in the textbook, not like a wobbly guess.

When the phone plan day came, Ms. Gupta gave them a plan with a fifteen-dollar starting fee plus three dollars per gigabyte. Marika frowned at her empty grid, but Vincent plotted the first point straight up the y-axis, at fifteen, then climbed by threes. "The fee is the starting point," he told her, and she copied his method, her line rising past his. At the top of the grid their two lines formed a small plateau before the paper ran out of room, and Marika laughed and taped a second sheet to the edge of the first.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Rotating crops, so the same plant family is not grown in the same spot year after year, helps keep soil pests and diseases from building up.
story:
Every April, Mia dragged the same three pots onto the same corner of the balcony and planted tomatoes, because her grandfather had done it that way and because tomatoes were the only vegetable her little brother would eat without staging a protest. This April, the seedlings came up spindly and yellow, then wilted at the stems one by one. By May she had lost two pots, and she sat on the balcony rail with her chin in her hands, glaring at the third.

"Maybe they're sad," said Viktor, who had come over to steal her wi-fi and stayed to watch the disaster. "Plants can be sad. My aunt talks to hers."

"Plants can't be sad," Mia said, though she had whispered "please" to the survivor that morning. She turned the wilted stem in her fingers and noticed something: the soil in that corner smelled flat, almost sour, and last year's stems had rotted the same way, in the same spot. She tried to distinguish this year's sickness from last year's by size or colour, and she couldn't. It was identical. Same corner, same disease, two years running.

The clue came from Ms. Schneider upstairs, who grew peppers along her railing like a string of lanterns. "My father moved his tomatoes to a new bed every single year," she said over the rail, handing down a dish of lemon cake. "He never put the same family in the same place twice. He called it rotating crops." Mia chewed on that along with the cake. If the same plant family kept going back to the same spot year after year, something in the soil built up and sickened them. She couldn't see it, but the pattern was there in her dead stems.

So she ran a test. She moved the surviving tomato to the opposite end of the balcony, dumped the old corner soil, and planted beans there instead, since beans were not in the tomato family. She drew a chart with arrows and labelled it THE ROTATION SCHEDULE, and underneath she wrote "fundamental rule: never same family, same spot." Viktor pointed out that one plant in one corner was not exactly a giant experiment. "That's true," Mia said. "But if my tomato lives over there and dies over here, that's a hundred percentage of the evidence I need." Viktor said that wasn't how percentages worked, and she threw a peat pellet at him.

By June the tomato had thickened into a green rope with tiny yellow flowers, while the beans in the old corner poked up cheerful and untouched. Mia knocked on Ms. Schneider's door with a bag of bean sprouts and a slice of her brother's abandoned birthday cake, because Ms. Schneider had once mentioned she loved cake and lived alone. "Next year the beans move and the tomatoes come back," Mia announced. Ms. Schneider saluted with her fork. "Your grandfather would be proud," she said. "Though he'd probably want a bigger cake."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The plain-folks technique presents a politician or company as ordinary, everyday people, so the audience trusts them as "one of us."
story:
Lauren had forty dollars of birthday money in her pocket, and the running shoes she wanted cost fifty-five. She stood in the middle of the mall food court, listening to the sizzle of the pretzel stand and smelling cinnamon and floor wax, drafting a plan in her head. If she could convince her mom to cover the last fifteen dollars, the shoes would be hers by dinner.

That was when she saw the giant screen above the shoe store. A famous sprinter, the one from the Olympics, held up the exact shoes Lauren wanted and said they made her feel unstoppable. Below the screen, a line of kids waited outside the store door, and a voice boomed that these were the shoes everyone was talking about. Everyone. Lauren felt her feet move toward the line before her brain caught up.

"What are you doing?" Aurora asked, appearing beside her with a smoothie. "You said you were saving for the green ones from the other store."

"I know, but look. That's the sprinter. And everyone's buying these."

Evie tilted her head at the screen. "Last month that same sprinter sold the headphones that broke in a week. Remember?" Lauren did remember. She also remembered the poster from the school election in October, when a candidate had put up a picture of himself eating cafeteria lasagna like a regular kid, and everyone voted for him before anyone asked what his plan actually was. He had turned out to have no plan at all. Mr. Nolan had muttered something about it in the hallway afterward, a phrase Lauren hadn't understood at the time: plain-folks.

She looked back at the store. A second poster showed the shoe company's owner in old jeans, grilling burgers in a backyard, with words like honest and real printed underneath. Honest. Real. Loaded words, the kind her English teacher had circled on their persuasive-writing worksheet, words that made you feel instead of think. And behind the counter, she noticed, a clerk was telling every customer the same thing: "You're the tenth person today to buy these."

"Test something for me," Lauren said. She walked to the counter and asked, "Are these actually better than the green ones at the other store, or just more popular?"

The clerk blinked. "Honestly? Same factory. The green ones cost less."

Aurora laughed so hard she nearly dropped her smoothie. "They got you with the famous lady, the big line outside, and the guy in the jeans. All of it."

The committee in Lauren's head was not unanimous. Part of her still wanted the popular shoes, the ones with the line and the screen and the sprinter's smile, because part of her remembered exactly how it felt to want what everyone wanted. But another part remembered the candidate with the lasagna, and how trusting him as one of us had gotten the whole grade nothing.

At the other store she found the green ones, forty-two dollars, and held them up to the light. The rubber smelled like a new eraser, and when she bent the sole it flexed the same way the expensive pair had.

"They even match your jacket," Evie said.

Lauren counted out the money, then paused and turned to Aurora. "Eight dollars left. Pretzel?"

They walked back toward the cinnamon smell, and Aurora said, "So the jeans guy in the poster, that one's called plain-folks. Mr. Nolan said it. Making a big shot look ordinary so you trust him."

"Like the lasagna guy," Lauren said, and took a bite.
