activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word diaspora comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors.
story:
Annabelle got to the community centre at nine fifty, ten minutes before the culture festival opened, and the banner over Loick's table still had a problem. It read "Filipino Diaspora Club" in tall red letters, and already two people had stopped, squinted at the last word.

"What does that even mean?" asked a man carrying a toddler.

"Um," said Loick.

"We're supposed to open at ten," Annabelle said. "Ms. Zhu said every table needs a poster that explains the group, and ours has to be up by then." The deadline was real: Ms. Zhu was walking the rows right now with her clipboard, and last year she'd made Eddie's chess club take down a poster with a spelling error.

Eddie arrived with the tape. "I looked up diaspora last night," he said, "but I fell asleep before the page loaded."

"I think I know it," Annabelle said slowly. She'd heard her grandmother use it at a wedding once, and she'd asked about it afterward, which was unusual for her, because she usually let big words pass by. "It's from a Greek word. It means scattering. Like seeds." She traced the shape of it in the air. "So a diaspora is a people living spread out, far away from where their ancestors came from."

Loick blinked. "So the banner's saying Filipinos here, and in Canada, and in Dubai, all scattered from the islands?"

"Right. But nobody at this table can say that out loud, which is the problem. The man with the toddler just left without signing up." Annabelle grabbed a marker and the back of an old pizza box. "Test it. We write it plain, and we see if people stop."

Eddie held the cardboard steady while she printed: "Scattered across the world, far from our ancestors' homeland. That's what diaspora means. Ask us anything." She taped it below the banner at 9:58.

Ms. Zhu came by at 10:07 with her clipboard. She read both signs, then the sign-up sheet, which already had four names on it, including the man with the toddler. "Good," she said, and moved on.

By eleven, the sheet had nineteen names, and Loick's mother had brought out a pot of soup. Annabelle found a note in the club's mailbox at the front desk, addressed in pencil to the table with the pizza-box sign: "My family is from Ghana and I never knew there was a word for all of us everywhere. Can I come to the next meeting? Signed, a girl from the Trinidad table."

Annabelle read it twice, then walked it back to Loick without saying anything, and watched his face as he read it.

"Tell her yes," he said, and went to ladle more soup.

activity: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
knowledge_domain: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
fact: The tuning fork, which rings at one steady pitch, was invented in 1711 by John Shore, a trumpeter at the English royal court.
story:
Backstage at the concert hall, Luca's violin was broken and nobody knew it. Not cracked, not smashed, just quietly wrong, because his A string had slipped flat sometime between the school bus and the warm-up room. He discovered it when he played the open string and it landed with a sad, sagging thud instead of a clean note.

"Use the piano in the wings," said Maxine, who was tuning her own violin against it. Luca tried, but the piano was so far away and the hallway so noisy that he couldn't hear if he matched it or not. Lyna covered her ears. "Somebody's kettle is boiling," she announced. "It's Luca."

Then Luca remembered the small metal fork in his grandfather's old case, the one his grandfather had pressed into his hand last weekend. "This is a tuning fork," his grandfather had said, and told him the story that went with it: it was invented in 1711 by John Shore, a trumpeter at the English royal court. Luca had thought it looked like a bent dinner fork with only two tines, something a hungry artisan might have made by accident. He dug it out of his backpack now and struck it against his knee.

Nothing. He struck it harder. Still nothing, and his knee began to sting. His heart picked up speed. Ms. Chukwu poked her head in and said five minutes to places, and the lineup of kids began to circulate through the warm-up room like fish in a too-small tank. Luca held the fork to his ear and held his breath. There it was, so faint he'd missed it, a thin silver hum at one steady pitch, exactly the pitch his grandfather had made him memorize with his eyes shut.

He set the fork's stem against the body of the violin, and the hum bloomed loud enough to hear over everything. One peg, a slow turn, tiny adjustments, his ear testing each one against that ringing A. The string slid up, wavered, and then locked into place with a sound that felt like two puzzle pieces clicking.

"Fixed," Luca said.

"That's legitimate magic," said Lyna.

Ms. Chukwu called them to the stage. Luca put the fork in his shirt pocket, picked up his violin, and walked out into the lights.

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: NIST's password guidance tells systems not to require mixes of uppercase letters, numbers and symbols, because length adds more strength than those rules do.
story:
Hazel sat cross-legged on Bruce's living room floor with his laptop between them, because Bruce's ambition to run the fastest gaming club at school had somehow become her problem too. He was signing up for a new tournament site, and the password box had turned an ominous red. "It wants a symbol," Bruce groaned, typing G@m3r and then glaring when the bar stayed short.

"That's the weird part," Hazel said. "I read that the rules forcing uppercase and numbers and symbols actually don't help much. Length adds more strength than those rules do." She plucked a marshmallow from the bowl Bruce's mom had left them and popped it in her mouth. "There's this guidance, from NIST, that tells systems not to require mixes of uppercase letters, numbers and symbols at all."

Bruce looked skeptical, so Hazel tested it right there. She typed a long silly sentence, all lowercase, no symbols, no numbers, just lots and lots of letters. The strength bar climbed higher than his G@m3r had ever pushed it. "See? Twenty plain letters beat your seven fancy ones." Bruce abandoned his symbol and typed the name of his favorite sandwich spread, spelled out long, and the bar filled green. Hazel felt a flicker of envy that he'd thought of a passphrase that fast, since she was usually the clever one.

The site swallowed his new password and they went back to planning the tournament bracket. Half an hour later Bruce's phone buzzed with a message from Stephen, and Bruce read it out loud: "Dude, change your password on the club forum NOW. Someone logged in as me and posted garbage. I only ever used one password everywhere and I think that's how they got in." Bruce went pale. He clicked open his tournament account, then his forum account, then his game account, typing with flying fingers. Every single one had the same password on it, the old one, the symbol one.

"That's the other half," Hazel said quietly. "A password can be strong and still get stolen from one site. If you reuse it, it opens every other door too." She watched him hunch over the keyboard and slid the marshmallow bowl closer, because he looked like a person who needed marshmallows. He grabbed a handful without looking up.

They spent the next hour making new passphrases, each one long and plain and different, and Hazel made Bruce say each out loud once so he'd remember it as a phrase instead of a code. When they finished, a new message appeared from Stephen: "False alarm, guys. It was Ms. González. She's running a digital safety lesson for the club and wanted to see who reused passwords. Only three of us passed. Nice work, Hazel." Bruce stared at the screen, then at his row of fresh passphrases, and started to laugh. "We passed a test we didn't even know we were taking." Hazel held up a marshmallow in a silent toast.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: The Yom Kippur fast lasts about 25 hours, from sunset one day until after nightfall the next.
story:
Harrison stood in his grandmother's kitchen holding a plate of honey cake he was not allowed to eat. The cake was for after, for the meal that breaks the fast, and everyone kept saying the word "after" as if it were a place far away. Tonight was the start of Yom Kippur, and this year, at eleven, Harrison had decided he would try fasting the way the grown-ups did. His mother had said he could do it for part of the day if it got hard, but he wanted the whole thing. He just did not know how long the whole thing was.

"How long does it actually last?" he asked his cousin Bianca, who was leaning against the counter, also not eating cake, but only because she was saving room.

"Ask your mom," Bianca said. "She's the one with the calendar."

His mother was stirring a pot of soup. "From sunset tonight until after nightfall tomorrow," she said. "About twenty-five hours."

"Twenty-five?" Harrison frowned. "A day is twenty-four. Where does the extra hour come from?" His mother only smiled and went back to the soup, which was deeply irritating. He found a napkin and a pencil and worked it out at the table. If it began at sunset, and sunset happened a little earlier every day in autumn, then tomorrow's nightfall would arrive slightly sooner than today's sunset had left. But the fast did not stop at sunset. It stopped after nightfall, and the sky took its time going dark. That was the missing piece. Sunset to sunset was about a day, and nightfall lagged behind sunset by roughly an hour, which stacked the extra hour on the end. He turned the napkin around to show Bianca. "It's not a longer day. It's a day plus the time it takes the sky to finish."

"Very credible," said Melodie, Bianca's little sister, who had wandered over. "Except you wrote 'nitefall' with no h."

Later, while the family rested, Harrison's grandmother handed him a folded note, because she had lost her voice to a virus that week and the doctor had not authorized her to talk above a whisper at the table. The note said: "When I was your age I broke my fast on a pickle. Nobody saw. You don't have to be perfect on your first try, boychik." He laughed so hard he had to stuff his knuckle in his mouth, since the house was quiet for prayer.

The next evening he stood in the driveway with Bianca and Melodie, all three of them watching the western sky like scientists waiting for a result. The sun went down. Harrison's stomach growled, and he held up one finger. Not yet. The blue faded to gray, then to a soft black, and finally the first stars came out. Somewhere inside, his grandmother was already slicing the honey cake.

"There," Bianca said. "Nightfall. Twenty-five hours, kid."

Harrison ran for the door.

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Yawning is contagious: seeing someone else yawn often makes people yawn too.
story:
Vincent had never slept anywhere but his own room, so he packed his bag like he was preparing for something aggressive: two flashlights, three snacks, and a folded note his mom had slipped in at the last minute. "Open this if you get homesick," she had said, which almost made him feel homesick right there in the driveway. At Maddex's house the evening went fine until lights-out, when Maddex and Rachael, who was already there in her sleeping bag by the window, kept whispering and giggling and flopping around. Nobody was going to sleep. Vincent remembered something his older cousin had mentioned once, that seeing someone else yawn often makes people yawn too. He could not see whether it was true, but he could test it.

He let out a long, deliberate yawn, the kind that made his jaw click. Within a minute, Rachael yawned mid-sentence, and then Maddex yawned so wide he knocked his water bottle off the mattress. "Quit it," Maddex mumbled, yawning again as he said it. Vincent waited a bit, then yawned once more, quieter this time. Rachael's eyes were already half shut. He tried a third time and nobody copied it, because both of them had drifted off, faces slack, the closet door throwing a thin stripe of shadow across the floor. It had worked, though he could not exactly prove how; he had only the before and the after.

He still felt a small hollow spot in his chest, so he unfolded the note under his blanket with the smaller flashlight. His mom's handwriting slanted uphill: "The commerce of the corner store was slow today, so I bought you the orange soda you like. It is in the fridge for tomorrow. I did not disclose this to Maddex's mom because it is our secret. Sleep well. Love, Mom." Vincent smiled into his pillow.

He decided he would save the soda for after breakfast, and he would yawn at Maddex over the table just to watch it happen again. Outside, a car passed, and its headlights swept slowly across the ceiling and away.

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: The downbeat is the first beat of each bar, which a conductor shows with a downward stroke of the hand or baton.
story:
Backstage smelled like paint, because the school had spent all fall trying to renovate the old auditorium and had run out of time halfway through. Benjamin stood between Yann and Ashlynn in the choir line, gripping his folder so hard the paper crinkled. Through the curtain he could hear the piano, and a thin stripe of stage light cut across the floor like the equator, dividing the bright half from the dark half where he stood waiting.

His problem was simple and enormous: he had never performed before, and he could not hold a count. In rehearsal he always lost his place somewhere after verse two, and Ms. Das had marked his part with three red stars, which meant "danger." Ashlynn had leaned over during warm-up and whispered, "Just watch her hand. The downbeat is the first beat of each bar, the downward stroke." Benjamin had nodded, but he hadn't really understood what she meant.

The curtain swept open. Rows of parents sat in the renovated seats, faces pale and watery in the stage lights. The piano started, the choir came in, and everything went fine until the middle section, when a cough in the front row knocked the count right out of Benjamin's head. Bar? Verse? He had no idea. Panic climbed his throat.

Then he remembered Ashlynn's whisper. He stopped guessing and watched Ms. Das. Her hand rose, then dropped, and on each drop the choir sang a new syllable, the first beat of the bar, exactly as Ashlynn had said. Down, up, down, up, like a steady pendulum. He counted the strokes, waited for the drop that landed on his red-starred word, and opened his mouth.

His voice slid in with everyone else's, right on time. Nobody in the audience would ever know. Yann, singing beside him on the parallel riser step, gave a tiny nod without looking over, and Ms. Das's hand went on falling and rising, falling and rising, all the way to the final chord.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date.
story:
The food bank had taken over the library's basement meeting room on Saturday mornings, and Austin's first job was sorting donations at the table by the mystery shelf. Ayaan, who had volunteered since September, worked beside him, stacking cans and checking boxes. The room smelled of old paper and cardboard, and somewhere above them a heater ticked like a slow clock.

Austin had signed up because he wanted the hours for school credit, but mostly because he liked the idea of figuring things out. Now he watched Ayaan lift a box of cereal, squint at it, and drop the whole thing into the bin marked TRASH.

"Whoa," Austin said. "What's wrong with it?"

"It's expired. One day past the date. We have to throw out anything past its date."

Austin picked a box out of the trash and turned it over. "Best if used by," he read slowly. Something about the wording bothered him, the way a word choice bothers you in a sentence you've heard a hundred times. "It doesn't say expires on. It says best if used by."

Ayaan rolled his eyes. "Don't try your lawyer logic on me. Rules are rules."

"It's not logic yet," Austin said. "It's a hunch." He looked around the room. Across the basement, Ms. Warsame, the librarian who ran the program, was handing bags of rice to a woman with two kids. The kids were touching the spines of picture books someone had set out on the waiting table. Austin noticed something else too: the trash bin already held three more boxes of cereal, all tossed that morning. If the rule Ayaan followed was right, the food bank was throwing away a lot of perfectly good food. If it was wrong, someone in this neighborhood was going without cereal for no reason.

He waited until the line thinned, then carried two of the rescued boxes to Ms. Warsame. "Can I ask about these?" Before she could answer, he spotted a printed sheet taped to the sign-in table, a guideline page for volunteers. He read it, and his stomach did a small flip. There it was, in plain print: the USDA says a "best if used by" date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date.

"It's a quality date," Austin said, holding up the sheet. "Not a safety date. The cereal's just, like, one day less fresh."

Ayaan crossed his arms. "So you're saying I trashed four boxes for nothing?"

"I'm not going to accuse you," Austin said. "You were following what you thought was the rule. But the rule's different."

Ms. Warsame read the page herself, then looked at the trash bin, then at the three full shopping carts still waiting to be sorted. She pulled a marker from her pocket and wrote a note on the sorting table, big enough that nobody could miss it. "New rule for the whole morning," she said, and pointed at the cart of donations. "Start with the dairy cooler, boys. That part really is about safety."

Austin grabbed a crate of milk cartons, and Ayaan, still muttering about the cereal, snatched up the thermometer.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through an extra loop of tubing, making the air column longer and the note lower.
story:
Florence sat on her bedroom floor with the rented trumpet across her lap, staring at it like it had insulted her family. Three valves. That was it. Three little buttons, and yet the band book promised she could play dozens of notes. Her cat, Walrus, watched from the laundry basket with what looked like pity.

"Three buttons," she told him. "My video game controller has like twelve and it only makes one character jump."

She pressed the middle valve down and blew. A note came out, lower than before. She let go and blew again. Higher. She tried the first valve, then the third, then two at once, and slowly a suspicion formed: the more valves she pushed, the lower the note sank. It was almost like the buttons weren't changing anything inside, just sending her air the long way around.

She grabbed her flashlight and peered into the bell of the trumpet. The tubing coiled back on itself like a brass snail. She pressed the second valve and followed the loops with her finger, and there it was. Pushing the valve opened a detour, an extra loop of tubing, so her air had to travel farther before it escaped. Longer trip, lower note.

"Elly owes me a cookie," she announced to Walrus.

The next afternoon, Elly and Atticus came over, and Florence made them close their eyes and listen while she played the same pitch with different valve combinations. Atticus guessed wrong twice and then gasped when she showed him the tubing trick, tracing the air's path with her finger.

"So more tubing means lower?" Elly said.

"Exactly. Longer path, lower note."

Atticus picked up the trumpet and pressed all three valves, puffing out his cheeks like a bullfrog. The note that came out was so low and wobbly that Walrus fled the room in horror. Florence laughed so hard she had to coordinate herself back onto the chair.

"It's ironic," Atticus said. "I finally find an instrument with only three buttons, and it's still impossible."

"Almost impossible," Florence said. She lifted the trumpet, took a breath, and let a clean, clear G ring out through the open window.

fact: Practicing a speech out loud with a timer matters because reading silently is faster than speaking, so a speech often runs longer than expected.
story:
Alice's note cards said two minutes. She had read her speech about the school garden six times at her desk, and every time it took her about a minute and a half. She told Jolene it was fine.

Jolene sat on the stage steps in the empty auditorium and held up her phone. "Ms. Van Dijk wants the hook, three points, and the closing, and she cuts you off at two minutes. Time it for real. Out loud."

"Reading it counts," Alice said.

"Just do it."

Alice stood at the front of the stage and started. Her hook was a question about where cafeteria carrots came from. Then the three points, one about compost, one about the raised beds, one about the harvest lunch. Her voice sounded strange in the big room, and she slowed down more than she meant to, letting each sentence land.

"Stop," Jolene said. "Two minutes. You just started your third point."

Alice looked at her cards. Half the speech was still in her hand. "I read the whole thing in ninety seconds. Sitting. Silent."

"That's the problem, I think. Reading silently is faster than speaking. You can't hear the length until you say it." Jolene waved the phone. "Again."

They ran it twice more. Both times the speech ran long, by almost the same amount, so Alice worked out a rule: whatever the silent reading clocked, she should add to it. She crossed out two sentences about the compost temperatures, and she trimmed the story about the raccoon that got into the beds, though it hurt to cut her favorite part.

At class the next day, Ms. Van Dijk called her name. Alice gave the hook, the three points, and the closing, and Jolene raised one finger, then a second, and stopped.

"One amendment to my plan," Alice said afterward in the hall. "Every speech I ever write, I practice out loud with a timer. It's the only feasible way to know the real length."

Jolene pocketed her phone. "Then you owe me the raccoon story at lunch."
